Mycobacterium terrae: Laboratory studies have shown that all six isolates from a single center and over 90% of an additional 22 isolates of the Mycobacterium terrae complex are susceptible to ciprofloxacin and sulfonamides. Recent findings also indicate that 11 isolates of this complex are susceptible to linezolid. 2. Mycobacterium szulgai: This organism is susceptible in vitro to most antituberculous drugs, including quinolones and newer macrolides. For extrapulmonary infections, a combination of antituberculous medications based on susceptibility testing is recommended for 4–6 months. 3. Mycobacterium smegmatis: For mild disease, the preferred treatment is oral doxycycline combined with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. For severe disease, intravenous amikacin or imipenem is recommended. 4. Mycobacterium mucogenicum: In vitro susceptibility includes aminoglycosides, cefoxitin, clarithromycin, minocycline, doxycycline, quinolones, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and imipenem. 5. Mycobacterium malmoense: In vitro susceptibility includes ethambutol, ethionamide, kanamycin, and cycloserine, while resistance is noted to isoniazid (INH), streptomycin, rifampin, and capreomycin. For pulmonary infections, the preferred regimen includes INH, rifampin, ethambutol, with or without quinolones and macrolides. 6. Mycobacterium immunogenum: This organism is susceptible to amikacin and clarithromycin but resistant to ciprofloxacin, doxycycline, cefoxitin, tobramycin, and sulfamethoxazole. Optimal therapy is unknown, and treatment is challenging due to extensive antibiotic resistance. 7. Mycobacterium leprae: For patients weighing less than 12 kg, the preferred regimen is oral dapsone (1–2 mg/kg/day) and rifampin (150 mg) for 12–24 months. For paucibacillary leprosy (skin smear-negative), the regimen includes rifampin (600 mg orally once a month for 6 months) and dapsone (100 mg orally daily for 6 months). Severe cases with numerous nodules, fever, or visceral involvement may require prednisolone (30–40 mg/day orally for 1–2 weeks, then tapered over 12 weeks). Alternative regimens include clofazimine or thalidomide. For reversal reactions, prednisolone starting at 40 mg/day orally, tapered over 12 weeks, is preferred. 8. Mycobacterium xenopi: The cornerstone of therapy includes clarithromycin, rifampin, and ethambutol, continued until the patient has maintained negative sputum cultures for 12 months. For pulmonary disease, the preferred regimen includes INH, rifabutin or rifampin, ethambutol, clarithromycin, with or without streptomycin. A quinolone, preferably moxifloxacin, may substitute one of the antituberculous drugs. 9. Mycobacterium ulcerans: Preulcerative lesions may be treated with excision and primary closure, rifampin monotherapy, or heat therapy. Established ulcers often require surgical debridement and skin grafting, as most antimycobacterial agents are ineffective. To control complications, clarithromycin and rifampin are preferred. 10. Swine influenza: For severe or progressive illness, oseltamivir (150 mg orally twice daily) is recommended. Treatment duration depends on clinical response, and therapy should continue until the infection resolves or clinical improvement is satisfactory. If oseltamivir is unavailable, inhaled zanamivir or intravenous zanamivir (if available) is recommended. Peramivir IV may be considered as an alternative. Severely immunosuppressed patients may require antiviral chemoprophylaxis with oseltamivir or zanamivir. 11. Mycobacterium simiae: The preferred regimen includes clarithromycin, moxifloxacin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. 12. Mycobacterium fortuitum: In vitro susceptibility includes amikacin, ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin, sulfonamides, cefoxitin, imipenem, clarithromycin, and doxycycline. For serious skin, bone, and soft tissue infections, at least two agents with in vitro activity should be administered for a minimum of 4 months, with 6 months recommended for bone infections. 13. Mycobacterium scrofulaceum: Susceptibility data are lacking, and standard treatment regimens are controversial. Susceptibility testing is essential for confirmed disease-producing isolates. 14. Mycobacterium marinum: In vitro susceptibility includes rifampin, rifabutin, ethambutol, clarithromycin, sulfonamides, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. For osteomyelitis or deep structure infections, the preferred regimen includes clarithromycin, ethambutol, and rifampin. 15. Mycobacterium kansasii: For pulmonary disease, the preferred regimen includes rifampin, ethambutol, isoniazid, and pyridoxine for 12 months of negative sputum cultures. For rifampin-resistant disease, a three-drug regimen including clarithromycin, azithromycin, moxifloxacin, ethambutol, sulfamethoxazole, or streptomycin is recommended. 16. Mycobacterium gordonae: The preferred regimen includes ethambutol, rifabutin, clarithromycin, linezolid, or fluoroquinolones. 17. Mycobacterium genavense: Susceptibility includes amikacin, rifamycin, fluoroquinolones, streptomycin, and macrolides. Multidrug therapies including clarithromycin are more effective. 18. Mycobacterium haemophilum: In vitro susceptibility includes amikacin, clarithromycin, ciprofloxacin, rifampin, and rifabutin. For disseminated disease, the preferred regimen includes clarithromycin, rifampin, rifabutin, and ciprofloxacin. 19. Mycobacterium chelonae: For localized infections, clarithromycin (500 mg orally twice daily) is preferred. Alternative regimens include azithromycin, linezolid, or moxifloxacin combined with linezolid. Multidrug therapy is recommended to prevent resistance, with a total treatment duration of 6 months. 20. Mycobacterium celatum: The preferred regimen includes clarithromycin, ethambutol, ciprofloxacin, with or without rifabutin. 21. Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC): For severe nodular or fibrocavitary disease, the preferred regimen includes clarithromycin or azithromycin, rifampin or rifabutin, and ethambutol. Amikacin or streptomycin may be added early in therapy. For disseminated MAC disease, the regimen includes clarithromycin or azithromycin, ethambutol, with or without rifabutin. 22. Mycobacterium bovis: For pulmonary and most extrapulmonary diseases, the preferred regimen includes isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol for 2 months, followed by isoniazid and rifampin for 7 months. For serious disease, clarithromycin, amikacin, and cefoxitin or imipenem are recommended for 2–4 months. 23. Mycobacterium tuberculosis: During the continuation phase, isoniazid and rifampicin are administered daily for 18 weeks. For drug-resistant cases, alternative agents such as ethionamide, cycloserine, or para-aminosalicylic acid may be used. 24. Bacteroides fragilis: Preferred regimens include ampicillin-sulbactam or tigecycline. Alternative regimens include ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, ciprofloxacin, or TMP-SMX. 25. Vibrio vulnificus: Immediate treatment is critical. The preferred regimen includes doxycycline and ceftazidime. A single-agent regimen with a fluoroquinolone is also effective. 26. Vibrio parahaemolyticus: Mild cases typically do not require treatment. Severe cases may be treated with tetracycline or ciprofloxacin. 27. Vibrio cholerae: For pregnancy, erythromycin or azithromycin is preferred. 28. Treponema pallidum (Syphilis): Pregnant women should receive penicillin appropriate for their stage of infection. Infants with congenital syphilis require aqueous crystalline penicillin G for 10 days. 29. Leptospira: The preferred regimen is doxycycline (200 mg orally once weekly). 30. Borrelia recurrentis: For tick-borne relapsing fever, doxycycline is preferred. For louse-borne relapsing fever, a single dose of tetracycline is recommended. 31. Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease): For acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans, doxycycline, amoxicillin, or cefuroxime axetil is recommended for 21 days.
